subtype: Approach: adjusting scope after a slow start [Revision]
passage: By day four Pooja's sprint chart looked wrong. She had planned a full budgeting app: login, charts, reminders, shared accounts, export. Only login and half the chart worked. In her Pune flat she sat back and counted what remained: three days, and at her speed, roughly one feature a day. "That's two features too many," she said to her flatmate Nandini, who was folding laundry. "I'm cutting reminders and shared accounts." "Won't it look small?" "It'll look finished." She deleted two lines from the plan and moved the charts to the top. On day seven, the app ran end to end. It did less than she first wanted, and she could show it.

qa.q: Which two features did Pooja cut?
qa.a: Pooja cut reminders and shared accounts.

qa.q: What is Pooja feeling when she sees the chart on day four?
qa.a: Pooja feels worried and a bit disappointed that the plan is too big, but she stays practical.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Pooja use to avoid overbuilding next time, and why?
qa.a: She could estimate each feature's time on day one and plan with a smaller list, because early estimates would have shown the plan was too large.

qa.q: How does Nandini see Pooja's decision?
qa.a: Nandini asks whether the app will look small and hears that it will look finished, so Nandini's doubt is answered by the promise of a working result.

grounding: Shows noticing a too-large plan on day four and dropping features to keep the core working so the sprint ends with a running app.

subtype: Approach: adjusting scope after a slow start [Revision]
passage:
'Day four, Tushar. Day four and the login doesn't even work.' Tanuja turned the laptop toward him.
'What was the plan again?'
'Seven days. Login, profile photos, chat, and the bus timetable for our campus.'
'Which one do people actually need?'
Tanuja paused. 'The timetable. Everyone asks me when the last bus is.'
'So what happens if login and chat wait?'
'Then it's... just a timetable.'
'A timetable that works. Versus four half-things on Saturday.'
She stared at the screen, then opened her notes and struck through two lines. 'Fine. No chat. No photos either. Timetable first, login only if there's time.'
'You're sure about photos?'
'Sure. Three days left.'
On Saturday evening, Tushar checked the last bus from his phone: 9:40, from the main gate. It was right.

qa.q: What four things were in Tanuja's original plan?
qa.a: Login, profile photos, chat, and the bus timetable for the campus.

qa.q: How was Tanuja feeling on day four, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was frustrated and worried, turning the laptop toward Tushar and repeating 'day four' because even the login did not work.

qa.q: What else could Tanuja have done on day one to avoid this?
qa.a: Pick the one feature people need most and build it first, adding extras only once it works.

qa.q: How does the smaller app look to Tushar on Saturday?
qa.a: To Tushar it is simply useful: the last bus time is right, and nobody misses the chat.

grounding: Shows a student realising on day four that the app is too big, dropping two features, and ending the week with a working core.

subtype: Approach: adjusting scope after a slow start [Revision]
passage:
The plan I wrote for the dance society app was beautiful: event calendar, ticket booking, member profiles and a photo gallery, all in ten days. I'm Sudha, and I had only just started learning the app framework.
By day four I had a calendar that crashed if two events fell on one date, and nothing else. That evening Vidya, the society secretary, asked if we could still use it for the fest. I heard myself say 'maybe' and knew that meant no.
So I sat on the hostel stairs with my plan and asked one question: what does the fest actually need? A calendar, and a way to see who is performing when. I crossed out booking and the gallery. Profiles became a plain list.
For the next six days I only fixed and polished the calendar. It went live two days before the fest. Nobody asked about the gallery.

qa.q: What happened on day four when two events fell on one date?
qa.a: The calendar crashed if two events fell on one date.

qa.q: What did Sudha feel after answering Vidya with 'maybe'?
qa.a: Sudha felt uneasy and a bit ashamed, knowing 'maybe' really meant no, and that pushed a rethink of the plan.

qa.q: Which approach would have suited Sudha better from the start?
qa.a: Planning just the calendar first and adding booking or a gallery only once it worked would have avoided losing four days.

qa.q: How does the app look to Vidya and the dance society at the fest?
qa.a: For them it works and does what they need; they can see who is performing when and do not miss the extras.

grounding: Shows a student noticing on day four that the planned app is too big, dropping two features, and finishing with a working calendar.
